step_1_memory_layout.label: Step 1: Memory Layout & References
step_1_memory_layout.description: Understand how languages represent objects in memory and expose references/pointers differently.
step_1_memory_layout.adapterInsight: Notice how C++ requires explicit `new`/`delete` or smart pointers, Go uses value semantics by default with optional pointers, and Python hides allocation entirely. TypeScript inherits from JavaScript's garbage collection.

codes.python:
# Common baseline
x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x                             # same object reference
y.append(4)

# Additional identity/reference cues
a = {"v": 1}
b = dict(a)                       # shallow copy
assert a is not b                 # different object identity

# Additional mutability cues
coords = (1, 2)                   # immutable tuple
items = [1, 2]                    # mutable list

step_2_collections_generics.label: Step 2: Collections & Generics
step_2_collections_generics.description: Learn how each language optimizes arrays, maps, and expresses generic (parameterized) types.
step_2_collections_generics.adapterInsight: Compare C++ templates vs Python's duck typing vs TypeScript's generics. See how Go's `interface{}` differs from Java's `Object`-based erasure. Scala uses type classes for ad-hoc polymorphism. Trade-off lens: ordered/tree containers give stable order and typically O(log n) updates; unordered/hash containers prioritize average O(1) lookup; queue/stack families optimize access pattern (FIFO/LIFO) over random access.

codes.python:
# Common baseline
nums: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
freq: dict[str, int] = {"a": 1}
def first(v): return v[0]

# Ordered-ish / sorted usage
records = [{"k": 2}, {"k": 1}]
records_sorted = sorted(records, key=lambda x: x["k"])

# Unordered / hash-based
unique = {1, 2, 3}
index = {"alice": 0, "bob": 1}

# Queue / stack / utility containers
from collections import deque, Counter, defaultdict
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
stack = [1, 2, 3]; stack.append(4); stack.pop()
cnt = Counter(["a", "b", "a"])
groups = defaultdict(list)

val freq: Map[String, Int] = Map("a" -> 1)
def first[T](v: Vector[T]): T = v.head

// Ordered / sorted
val sortedMap = scala.collection.immutable.SortedMap("b" -> 2, "a" -> 1)
val sortedSet = scala.collection.immutable.SortedSet(3, 1, 2)

// Hash-based defaults
val hashMap = scala.collection.immutable.HashMap("a" -> 1)
val hashSet = scala.collection.immutable.HashSet(1, 2, 3)

step_3_function_paradigm.label: Step 3: The Function Paradigm
step_3_function_paradigm.description: Learn how languages treat functions: as first-class values, callable objects, or structured procedures.
step_3_function_paradigm.adapterInsight: In Scala and TypeScript, functions are first-class. In C++, use `std::function`. In Go, functions are values passed as interface{}. Understand closures and how each captures environment.

step_4_error_philosophies.label: Step 4: Error Philosophies
step_4_error_philosophies.description: Compare how languages handle errors: exceptions, error returns, type-driven approaches, or panics.
step_4_error_philosophies.adapterInsight: Go and C++23 treat errors as values. Python, TypeScript, and Scala 2 use exceptions. Scala 3 uses Option/Either for type-safe error handling. Pick the right pattern for your context.

step_5_type_system_interfaces.label: Step 5: Type System & Interfaces
step_5_type_system_interfaces.description: Understand how each language defines contracts between types: nominal vs structural typing, traits, interfaces, and type classes.
step_5_type_system_interfaces.adapterInsight: C++ uses virtual dispatch (nominal) and concepts (structural, compile-time). Go interfaces are structural — any type satisfying the method set qualifies implicitly. TypeScript is also structural. Scala uses traits with explicit `extends` (nominal) but type classes (`given`/`using`) for ad-hoc structural polymorphism. Python uses duck typing at runtime.

step_6_strings_pattern_matching.label: Step 6: Strings & Pattern Matching
step_6_strings_pattern_matching.description: Explore string ergonomics and how each language expresses branching on values or structure — from switch/case to destructuring match expressions.
step_6_strings_pattern_matching.adapterInsight: C++ strings are mutable byte arrays; formatting requires `std::format` (C++20) or `snprintf`. Python and Go treat strings as immutable UTF-8 sequences. TypeScript template literals are concise. Scala/Kotlin pattern matching is exhaustive and works on case classes. Python 3.10+ `match` brings structural matching.

codes.python:
# String basics
name = "Alice"
greeting = f"Hello, {name}!"
upper = name.upper()

# Pattern matching (Python 3.10+)
match code:
    case 1: print("one")
    case 2: print("two")
    case _: print("other")

# Structural match
match point:
    case (0, 0): print("origin")
    case (x, 0): print(f"on x-axis at {x}")
codes.scala3:
// String basics
val name = "Alice"
val greeting = s"Hello, $name!"
val upper = name.toUpperCase

// Pattern match on values
code match
  case 1 => println("one")
  case 2 => println("two")
  case _ => println("other")

// Structural + guard
point match
  case (0, 0)       => "origin"
  case (x, 0)       => s"x-axis $x"
  case (x, y) if x == y => "diagonal"

step_7_concurrency_model.label: Step 7: Concurrency Model
step_7_concurrency_model.description: Compare the core concurrency primitives: OS threads, goroutines, async/await, and Futures/Promises.
step_7_concurrency_model.adapterInsight: C++ uses OS threads with mutexes/condition variables and `std::async` for task-based work. Go's goroutines are lightweight M:N user-space threads coordinated via channels. Python has the GIL: use `asyncio` for I/O concurrency or `multiprocessing` for CPU work. TypeScript/Node is single-threaded with an event loop — `async/await` suspends without blocking. Scala Futures run on an ExecutionContext (thread pool).

codes.python:
# asyncio — cooperative, single-threaded I/O concurrency
import asyncio
async def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0)   # yield control
    return url

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a"), fetch("b"))

# Thread for CPU / blocking work
from threading import Thread
t = Thread(target=lambda: print("from thread"))
t.start(); t.join()

step_8_io_serialization.label: Step 8: I/O & Serialization
step_8_io_serialization.description: Compare file I/O patterns, standard streams, and JSON serialization across languages.
step_8_io_serialization.adapterInsight: C++ I/O is buffered stream-based (`fstream`) with manual error checking. Python's `open()` + context manager is idiomatic. Go uses `os.Open` + `bufio` and separates concerns clearly. TypeScript (Node) has `fs.readFileSync`/`fs/promises`. JSON serialization is built-in for Python/TS/Go; C++ requires a library (nlohmann/json, etc.).

codes.python:
# File read
with open("data.txt") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

# JSON
import json
obj = json.loads('{"name": "Ada"}')
name = obj["name"]
out = json.dumps(obj, indent=2)

step_9_sorting_pipelines.label: Step 9: Sorting & Data Pipelines
step_9_sorting_pipelines.description: Compare how each language chains collection transforms — sorting, filtering, mapping, and reducing — and uses heaps for priority selection.
step_9_sorting_pipelines.adapterInsight: C++ uses STL algorithms (`std::sort`, `std::transform`, ranges in C++20). Python list/generator comprehensions and `sorted()` are concise. Go favors explicit loops with `sort.Slice`. TypeScript array methods (`.filter`, `.map`, `.reduce`) are chainable. Scala has the most expressive pipeline via `map`/`filter`/`foldLeft` on immutable collections and lazy `LazyList`.

codes.python:
nums = [5, 3, 1, 4, 2]
sorted_nums = sorted(nums)

# Pipeline via comprehension
doubled_evens = [x * 2 for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]

# Reduce
from functools import reduce
total = reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, nums, 0)

# Min-heap
import heapq
heap = nums[:]
heapq.heapify(heap)
top = heapq.heappop(heap)
codes.scala2:
val nums = List(5, 3, 1, 4, 2)
val sorted = nums.sorted

// Expressive pipeline
val result = nums
  .filter(_ % 2 == 0)
  .map(_ * 2)
  .foldLeft(0)(_ + _)

// Priority queue
import scala.collection.mutable
val pq = mutable.PriorityQueue[Int]()
nums.foreach(pq.enqueue(_))
val top = pq.dequeue()
codes.scala3:
val nums = List(5, 3, 1, 4, 2)
val sorted = nums.sorted

// Expressive pipeline
val result = nums
  .filter(_ % 2 == 0)
  .map(_ * 2)
  .foldLeft(0)(_ + _)

// Lazy evaluation
val lazy = LazyList.from(1).filter(_ % 2 == 0).take(5).toList

step_10_testability_di.label: Step 10: Testability & Dependency Inversion
step_10_testability_di.description: Learn how to design swappable seams: constructor injection, interface mocking, and test doubles — the practical application of SOLID's DIP.
step_10_testability_di.adapterInsight: The common thread: inject an abstraction, swap in a test double. C++ uses virtual interfaces or template policy injection. Go's small implicit interfaces make mocking trivial. Python replaces any callable at runtime. TypeScript uses structural interfaces — any matching shape works. Scala leverages traits and implicit/given for type class injection.
